rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revelation paused after the first five verses; during the pause Muhammad continued to see Gabriel and receive non-Qur’anic revelation, while the duration is not important.
rows.anchor: الوحي فتر بعد نزول الآيات الخمس الأوائل من هذه السورة وتلك الفترة الأولى

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhayli says the revelation pause lasted two years; Ibn Ashur considers that duration unlikely.
rows.anchor: كانت المدة سنتين ، وفيه بعد

rows.speaker: الحربي
rows.claim: Al-Harbi says before the Night Journey the Prophet prayed once before sunset, meaning Asr, and once before sunrise, meaning Fajr.
rows.anchor: ذكر الحربي أن الصلاة قبل الإسراء كانت صلاة قبل غروب الشمس

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: Yahya ibn Salam gives the same account and says the Night Journey and prescription of the five prayers occurred a year before the Hijra.
rows.anchor: وقال يحيى بن سلام مثله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The early prayer was a distinct, still-unregulated form of worship involving prostration, performed publicly; Abu Jahl objected and forbade it.
rows.anchor: بل كانت هيئة غير مضبوطة بكيفية وفيها سجود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rest of the surah followed the opening verses after a short interval, when the Prophet had begun praying and news of revelation had spread; consecutive recitation normally reflects consecutive revelation, and al-Alaq was the first surah revealed.
rows.anchor: الأصل في الآيات المتعاقبة في القراءة أن تكون قد تعاقبت في النزول إلا ما ثبت تأخره بدليل بين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The statement that the human transgresses when he considers himself self-sufficient introduces the account of the man who forbids prayer and its continuation through the command not to obey him.
rows.anchor: موقع المقدمة لما يرد بعده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes agree that the one who forbids the worshipper is Abu Jahl, who threatened to trample Muhammad’s neck if he saw him praying at the Kaaba; this was a threat meant to reach Muhammad, not a face-to-face prohibition.
rows.anchor: اتفقوا على أنه أريد به أبو جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Have you seen” expresses amazement at a known extraordinary event; seeing is intellectual, its second object is omitted and supplied by the final question in verse 14.
rows.anchor: تقال للذي يعلم أنه رأى حالا عجيبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative conveys astonishment through a rhetorical transfer: people ask for confirmation of something so extraordinary that it is hard to believe.
rows.anchor: فاستعمال الاستفهام في التعجيب مجاز مرسل في التركيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address may also describe visual witnessing of an actual event; the addressee of the question is unspecified.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن تكون الرؤية بصرية لأنها حكاية أمر وقع في الخارج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A servant” refers to the Prophet but deliberately generalizes him as any person devoted to God, making the prohibition itself astonishing regardless of the worshipper’s identity.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالعبد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم وإطلاق العبد هنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense pictures the extraordinary scene vividly although Abu Jahl’s prohibition had already occurred, and the omitted prohibited act is understood from the prayer context.
rows.anchor: لاستحضار الحالة العجيبة وإلا فإن نهيه قد مضى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A second hypothetical astonishment asks whether the forbidding man would also obstruct a servant who is rightly guided or commands piety.
rows.anchor: أتظنه ينهى أيضا عبدا متمكنا من الهدى فتعجب من نهيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Stopping prayer means stopping a devotional act, and thus stopping guidance; Abu Jahl might even forbid someone from commanding piety.
rows.anchor: من ينهى عن الصلاة وهي قربة إلى الله فقد نهى عن الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional particle, usually used when the condition is uncertain, matches the stance of the man who forbids the servant.
rows.anchor: وأتى بحرف الشرط الذي الغالب فيه عدم الجزم بوقوع فعل الشرط مجاراة لحال الذي ينهى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The vision verb is intellectual, with both objects omitted for concision; the previous servant identifies the first, and the previous prohibition supplies the second.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعولا فعل الرؤية اختصارا لدلالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Upon” is a metaphor of elevation for being firmly established in guidance, as in the cited description of believers as being upon guidance.
rows.anchor: للاستعلاء المجازي وهو شدة التمكن من الهدى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the conditionals, the hidden pronouns refer back to the servant, despite nearby pronouns referring to the forbidding man; context restores each pronoun to its proper antecedent.
rows.anchor: فإن السياق يرد كل ضمير إلى معاده كما في قول عباس بن مرداس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second object of “have you seen” is omitted and can be understood from verse 14 or from the earlier “forbids”; the implied question is whether he would forbid him too.
rows.anchor: إن كان على الهدى أو أمر بالتقوى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause is detached because it repeats the astonishment about several possible states of the same person.
rows.anchor: لوقوعها موقع التكرير لأن فيها تكرير التعجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause begins a fresh threat: if the man denies the call and turns away, should he think God does not know what he does? The first object of “have you seen” is omitted and refers to the forbidding man.
rows.anchor: جملة مستأنفة للتهديد والوعيد على التكذيب والتولي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhshari takes the question in verse 14 as the answer to the condition; al-Radi allows an interrogative answer without the expected fa, comparing another conditional question.
rows.anchor: ولم يعتبر وجوب اقتران جملة جواب الشرط بالفاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most grammarians, including al-Zamakhshari in al-Mufassal, require the fa; on their analysis the implicit answer is that God knows and will punish him, and verse 14 independently denies the offender’s ignorance.
rows.anchor: فأما قول جمهور النحاة والزمخشري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saying God sees him is an indirect threat of punishment; “knows” includes certainty, and the interrogative rebukes him for failing to know and protect himself from punishment.
rows.anchor: وكني بأن الله يرى عن الوعيد بالعقاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb “know” carries the sense of certainty, which accounts for its construction with “bi”.
rows.anchor: معنى يوقن فلذلك عدي بالباء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question suspends the verb “have you seen” from taking its object because an interrogative follows.
rows.anchor: هنا عن العمل لوجود الاستفهام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conditional predicts that Abu Jahl will deny the Prophet when called to Islam and turn away; God promises to give the Prophet justice against him.
rows.anchor: بأن أبا جهل سيكذبه حين يدعوه إلى الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The denial’s pronoun refers to the man who forbids prayer, while the object of “deny” is omitted because the preceding context identifies the servant he denies.
rows.anchor: وحذف مفعول { كذب } لدلالة ما قبله عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The object of God’s seeing is omitted to make the statement encompass every existent; divine seeing means knowledge of perceptible things.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالرؤية المسندة إلى الله تعالى تعلق علمه بالمحسوسات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second “kalla” reinforces the first; placing one at the start created suspense, and the closing position is the natural place for its counterpart.
rows.anchor: أكد الردع الأول بحرف الردع الثاني في آخر الجملة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning follows as a threat if the offender does not desist; the lām introduces an oath, its answer is “we will seize,” and the conditional answer is omitted.
rows.anchor: وأما جواب الشرط فمحذوف دل عليه جواب القسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Seizing means gripping and pulling forcefully; taking someone by the forelock signifies dragging him to punishment and humiliating him.
rows.anchor: والأخذ من الناصية أخذ من لا يترك له تمكن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The added bāʾ strengthens the sense of contact in the seizure; the light emphatic nūn commonly follows positive oaths and is written as an alif to reflect pausal pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وأكد ذلك السفع بالباء المزيدة الداخلة على المفعول لتأكيد اللصوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light emphatic nūn often enters affirmative oaths and is written as an alif in the muṣḥaf to reflect its pronunciation at pause.
rows.anchor: والنون نون التوكيد الخفيفة التي يكثر دخولها في القسم المثبت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite forelock is anaphoric, meaning the forelock of the man who forbids prayer; Kufan grammarians call the lām a substitute for the genitive pronoun, while Basrans posit an attachment for the lām’s complement.
rows.anchor: والتعريف في ( الناصية ) للعهد التقديري ، أي بناصيته ، أي ناصية الذي ينهى عبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A forelock, lying, sinful” is an indefinite appositive referring to the generic kind; describing it as lying and sinful is a rhetorical attribution to its owner, imagining his sins visible on his forelock.
rows.anchor: ووصف الناصية بالكاذبة والخاطئة مجاز عقلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports that Abu Jahl confronted Muhammad as he prayed at the Maqam, threatened him, and boasted that he had the largest council; the verses answer his threat to mobilize his people.
rows.anchor: ما رواه الترمذي والنسائي عن ابن عباس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The council is first the place where people assemble; it is called a council only while its members are gathered, and its daytime gathering contrasts with the nighttime “sāmir”.
rows.anchor: اسم للمكان الذي يجتمع فيه القوم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qusayy established a Quraysh council house around the Sacred Mosque for consultation and major affairs; the site was gradually incorporated into later mosque expansions.
rows.anchor: واتخذ قصي لندوة قريش دارا تسمى دار الندوة حول المسجد الحرام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Council” also means the people who gather there: Abu Jahl means the many people who sit with him as their leader, just as place-names can denote inhabitants.
rows.anchor: ويطلق النادي على الذين ينتدون فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The metonymic usage of a place for its people is supported by poetic uses of “majlis,” “maqāmāt,” and “majāmiʿ” for those who occupy them.
rows.anchor: نظير إطلاق المجلس على أهله في قول ذي الرمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to summon his council is a taunting challenge: if Abu Jahl calls them to attack, God will call angels to destroy them; the challenge was a Quranic miracle because neither Abu Jahl nor his supporters dared act.
rows.anchor: للتعجيز لأن أبا جهل هدد النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم بكثرة أنصاره

rows.speaker: أعرابية
rows.claim: An Arab woman praised a man as the master of his council and the support of those in need.
rows.anchor: أعرابية : ( سيد ناديه ، وثمال عافيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We will summon” answers the taunting imperative and is jussive as its response; the muṣḥaf spelling omits the wāw and future prefix to strengthen the verb.
rows.anchor: فإن دعا ناديه دعونا لهم الزبانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word “zabāniya” has several proposed plural forms, or may be a plural collective with no singular of the same form; it derives from forceful pushing, and refers to punishment angels, while also naming police assistants.
rows.anchor: بفتح الزاي وتخفيف التحتية جمع زباني بفتح الزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Kalla” rebuts the challenge and confirms that Abu Jahl will not carry it out.
rows.anchor: ردع لإبطال ما تضمنه قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The muṣḥaf omits a wāw after the ʿayn in “we will summon,” because it is joined in recitation rather than paused at a verse ending.
rows.anchor: في المصحف بدون واو بعد العين مراعاة لحالة الوصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing passage sums up the previous argument: the Prophet should keep praying in the Sacred Mosque and not fear Abu Jahl.
rows.anchor: هذا فذلكة للكلام المتقدم من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do not obey him” uses obedience metaphorically for fear or caution, meaning that Abu Jahl cannot harm the Prophet; the command to prostrate underscores prayer, and “draw near” praises its nearness to God.
rows.anchor: وأطلقت الطاعة على الحذر الباعث على الطاعة على طريق المجاز المرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The form “iqtarib” conveys effort and seeking: strive to draw near to God through prayer.
rows.anchor: عبر بصيغة الافتعال لما فيها من معنى التكلف والتطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening “inna” and verbal clause both reinforce the statement; its foregrounding restrictively counters the polytheists’ denial that the Quran was sent down by God.
rows.anchor: وكلاهما من طرق التأكيد والتقوي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The majestic first-person pronoun and attribution of the revelation to God honor the Quran; using its pronoun without an antecedent signals its fame among Muslims.
rows.anchor: وفي ضمير العظمة وإسناد الإنزال إليه تشريف عظيم للقرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may denote the entire Quran: “sent down” then begins the revelation with al-Alaq’s first five verses, which initiated a gradual process completed over twenty years; the whole is counted by its beginning, as mosque additions inherit the mosque’s prayer merit.
rows.anchor: ولكن لما كان جميع القرآن مقررا في علم الله تعالى مقداره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The placement of al-Qadr after al-Alaq in the muṣḥaf hints that the pronoun refers to the Quran whose revelation began with al-Alaq.
rows.anchor: ومن تسديد ترتيب المصحف أن وضعت سورة القدر عقب سورة العلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the pronoun refers only to the portion sent down that night, namely al-Alaq’s first five verses; every portion is called Quran, though some regard the whole-Quran pronoun for a part as metonymy.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الضمير عائدا على المقدار الذي أنزل في تلك الليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse states the first verses were revealed at night, as Aisha’s report in the two Ṣaḥīḥs says Muhammad worshipped in the cave at night; the angel apparently came after his worship, and he returned home at dawn after the first revelation near the night’s end.
rows.anchor: الذي يقتضيه حديث بدء الوحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Laylat al-qadr” is God’s name for the night when Quranic revelation began; the name was likely new to Muslims, so its first mention creates suspense before the question about it.
rows.anchor: اسم جعله الله لليلة التي ابتدىء فيها نزول القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Qadr” means honor and merit bestowed by God, who made the night a blessed beginning of revelation, as in the description of the blessed night in al-Dukhan.
rows.anchor: كما قال تعالى في سورة الدخان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article marks a genus, but the double definiteness makes “Night of Decree” function like a conventional title for this night.
rows.anchor: قصد جعل هذا المركب بمنزلة العلم لتلك الليلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since the Quran is said to have been revealed in Ramadan, this night was in Ramadan; authentic reports confirm it recurs among Ramadan nights every year.
rows.anchor: ولا شك أن المسلمين كانوا يعلمون ذلك إذ كان نزول هذه السورة قبل نزول سورة البقرة بسنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most reports place the first revelation on the seventeenth night of Ramadan; Ibn Ashur says he will discuss whether the night recurs on a fixed date or varies, falls anywhere in Ramadan or only its last ten nights, and is restricted to odd nights.
rows.anchor: كانت ليلة سبع عشرة من رمضان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honoring the night honors the Quran: God chose a blessed time for the revelation’s beginning, and choosing the best times signals the Quran’s high standing, as with the purified touching the scripture.
rows.anchor: اختار لابتداء إنزاله وقتا شريفا مباركا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “What has made you know” magnifies the night by suggesting its full merit is difficult to comprehend; the circumstantial wāw introduces this explanation.
rows.anchor: كلمة تقال في تفخيم الشيء وتعظيمه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “Night of Decree” where a pronoun was expected emphasizes identification and magnifies both the night and the Quran God chose to reveal then.
rows.anchor: فقصد الاهتمام بتعيينها ، فحصل تعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next clause begins to explain the ambiguity in verse 2; it is separated as an explanatory resumption or apposition, like the explanation of the steep path in al-Balad.
rows.anchor: فلذلك فصلت الجملة لأنها استئناف بياني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The night is better because it multiplies good deeds, answered prayers, charity’s reward, and communal blessing; times have no inherent merit from duration or weather, only from the good they enable, as human merit rests on piety.
rows.anchor: إنما هو بتضعيف فضل ما يحصل فيها من الأعمال الصالحة واستجابة الدعاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The number one thousand expresses abundance rather than a literal limit; “month” as the unit of abundance also suits the verse’s rhyme.
rows.anchor: وعدد الألف يظهر أنه مستعمل في وفرة التكثير

rows.speaker: مالك
rows.claim: Malik heard from trusted scholars that the Prophet was shown the lifespans of earlier peoples and feared his community would not match their deeds, so God gave it the Night of Decree, better than a thousand months.
rows.anchor: مالك إنه سمع من يثق به من أهل العلم يقول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating “Night of Decree” three times emphasizes the subject; three repetitions often conclude a pattern, as in another Quranic repetition and the line by ʿAdī.
rows.anchor: وقد تكرر هذا اللفظ ثلاث مرات والمرات الثلاث ينتهي عندها التكرير غالبا

rows.speaker: القاسم بن الفضل الحداني
rows.claim: A report attributed to al-Hasan says the Prophet saw the Umayyads on a pulpit, disliked it, and the surah’s thousand months refer to their rule; the narrator says they counted exactly a thousand months.
rows.anchor: القاسم بن الفضل الحداني عن يوسف بن سعد قال

rows.speaker: أبو عيسى الترمذي
rows.claim: Al-Tirmidhi grades the report about the Umayyads as strange and known only through this route; he notes a variant narrator name, calls al-Qasim trustworthy, and says Yusuf ibn Saʿd is unknown.
rows.anchor: قال أبو عيسى الترمذي ، هذا حديث غريب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir gives another version through al-Qasim from ʿIsa ibn Mazin; because accounts disagree about al-Qasim’s source and both named narrators are unknown, the transmission is unstable.
rows.anchor: وهذا يقتضي اضطرابا في هذا الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Neither version establishes that Yusuf ibn Saʿd heard the story from al-Hasan; even if reliable, he could merely be repeating a story, and al-Tabari’s version names the unknown ʿIsa ibn Mazin.
rows.anchor: ليس في سنده ما يفيد أن يوسف بن سعد سمع ذلك من الحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Kathir, citing his teacher al-Mizzi, and other expert scholars call the report munkar; Ibn Ashur sees fabricated propaganda, an implausible defense of al-Hasan, and no connection between the alleged vision and his response to criticism.
rows.anchor: واتفق حذاق العلماء على أنه حديث منكر صرح بذلك ابن كثير وذكره عن شيخه المزي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The report’s exact thousand-month count contradicts history: from al-Hasan’s surrender of the caliphate to Muʿawiya until the first Abbasid caliph al-Saffah’s accession was 1,092 months or more.
rows.anchor: ألف شهر واثنان وتسعون شهرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur concludes that al-Tirmidhi’s report is munkar, agreeing with al-Mizzi.
rows.anchor: والحاصل أن هذا الخبر الذي أخرجه الترمذي منكر كما قاله المزي

rows.speaker: ابن عرفة
rows.claim: Ibn ʿArafa calls the repetition of the phrase ending one clause at the start of the next “similarity of extremities,” illustrating it with Quran 24:35 and a poem by Layla al-Akhyaliyya.
rows.anchor: المحسن المسمى تشابه الأطراف وهو إعادة لفظ القافية

rows.speaker: ليلى الأخيلية
rows.claim: Layla al-Akhyaliyya’s repeated “شفاها” at the end of one verse and beginning of the next illustrates the rhetorical pattern Ibn ʿArafa identifies.
rows.anchor: شفاها من الداء العضال الذي بها غلام إذا هز القناة سقاها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clarification of the night’s merit implies that this recurring annual night has the virtue of the original, honoring the Quran, Prophet, religion, and community; the surah encourages good works, and authentic reports explain the thousand-month comparison.
rows.anchor: حصل منهما ما يدل دلالة بينة على أن الله جعل مثل هذه الفضيلة لكل ليلة من ليالي الأعوام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The present tense of “the angels descend” signals that their descent recurs in future years after the surah’s revelation.
rows.anchor: هذا التنزل متكرر في المستقبل بعد نزول هذه السورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dawn endpoint is included to identify the night’s duration and urge worshippers to continue good works until it ends.
rows.anchor: تعين أنه إدماج للتعريف بمنتهاها ليحرص الناس على كثرة العمل فيها قبل انتهائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first revelation night had already passed without anyone knowing except Muhammad, who received revelation at its end; recurring angelic descent and the stated endpoint show the virtue applies to matching nights every year.
rows.anchor: فلولا إرادة التعريف بفضل الليالي الموافقة لها في كل السنوات لاقتصر على بيان فضل تلك الليلة الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims should honor days of religious blessing as Moses was told to recall God’s days, making Laylat al-Qadr a festival of the Quran’s revelation; its date is hidden to encourage repeated good deeds, as Friday’s answered-prayer hour is hidden.
rows.anchor: وهذا تعليم للمسلمين أن يعظموا أيام فضلهم الديني وأيام نعم الله عليهم

rows.speaker: محي الدين بن العربي
rows.claim: Ibn al-ʿArabi’s mnemonic places the night on a Friday after mid-month and on an odd date; Ibn Ashur heard the lines from teachers but could not locate them, and his sunrise sign has not failed in his trials.
rows.anchor: وحفظت عن الشيخ محي الدين بن العربي أنه ضبط تعيينها باختلاف السنين بأبيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Tanazzalu” contracts the form tata-nazzalu by deleting one of its two tāʾs; the angels descend to earth carrying blessings.
rows.anchor: تتنزل فحذفت إحدى التاءين اختصارا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The Spirit” is Gabriel, who descends among the angels; God’s permission honors the Muslims with an angelic host including the most noble angel and recalls Gabriel’s first descent with revelation at Hira.
rows.anchor: أي ينزل جبريل في الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse provides a precedent for processions commemorating Islam’s great occasions, including those who contributed to their origin.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا أصل لإقامة المواكب لإحياء ذكرى أيام مجد الإسلام وفضله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “By their Lord’s permission” attaches to “descend” either as cause, permission to descend, or as accompaniment, with “permission” meaning what was permitted, as in the creation verse.
rows.anchor: أي يتنزلون بسبب إذن ربهم لهم في النزول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Min” in “from every affair” may explain the permission, mean “by” every affair under the causal reading, or mean “for the sake of” each decree God intends to execute.
rows.anchor: أي بإذن ربهم الذي هو في كل أمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Every” here means many important matters rather than an exhaustive set; the indefinite “affair” magnifies them as rewards for that night’s deeds.
rows.anchor: أي في أمور كثيرة عظيمة كقوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The affair here is normally distinct from the wise decree in al-Dukhan, though it may be the same matter expressed generally here and with qualification there.
rows.anchor: فإن لها شؤونا عديدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels’ descent is an explanatory resumption or appositional detail of the night’s being better than a thousand months; separation signals that it is one feature of that merit.
rows.anchor: موقع الاستئناف البياني أو موقع بدل الاشتمال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “It is peace until dawn” explains the affairs of verse 4 and prevents a mistaken inference that angels descend for punishment; here they implement good for Ramadan worshippers, a glad tiding.
rows.anchor: وهو كالاحتراس لأن تنزل الملائكة يكون للخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Salām” means safety, a verbal noun or its equivalent, and also greeting or praise; both meanings apply, covering forgiveness, abundant reward and answered prayers, as well as angels’ greetings to the night’s worshippers.
rows.anchor: مصدر أو اسم مصدر معناه السلامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite “salām” magnifies the peace, and making the night itself “peace” intensifies the predicate.
rows.anchor: وأخبر عن الليلة بأنها سلام للمبالغة لأنه إخبار بالمصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting “peace” restricts the night to peace, an emphatic claim that disregards what it brings to people who do not fast and worship.
rows.anchor: على المسند إليه لإفادة الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “peace” may command people to greet one another and make the night peaceful, with the raised verbal noun conveying permanence rather than a bare imperative.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يراد بالمصدر الأمر ، والتقدير : سلموا سلاما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an authentic report, the Prophet says he was about to tell the community the night of Decree when two men quarreled and it was lifted; he urges them to seek it on the ninth, seventh, and fifth remaining nights.
rows.anchor: ويشير إليه ما في الحديث الصحيح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Until dawn” limits the descent and peace and conveys that the whole night is filled with angels and safety, even though “night of Decree” can refer to only part of a night.
rows.anchor: والمقصود من الغاية إفادة أن جميع أحيان تلك الليلة معمورة بنزول الملائكة والسلامة

rows.speaker: سعيد بن المسيب
rows.claim: Saʿid ibn al-Musayyib says a person who attends the congregational evening prayer on the night of Decree has gained a share of it.
rows.anchor: فقد قال سعيد بن المسيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Until” extends the night past the dawn’s arrival, so Fajr prayer counts within it; this prevents people from treating its end like the end of fasting and gives them more time.
rows.anchor: لإدخال الغاية لبيان أن ليلة القدر تمتد بعد مطلع الفجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The endpoint also marks the end of angelic descent and of the good works arising from the night’s thousand-month merit, as well as the end of its peace.
rows.anchor: أن تلك غاية الليلة وغاية لما فيها من الأعمال الصالحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most readers pronounce matlaʿ with an open lām as a verbal noun meaning dawn’s appearance; al-Kisaʾi and Khalaf use a kasra, meaning the time of dawn.
rows.anchor: بفتح اللام على أنه مصدر ميمي ، أي طلوع الفجر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet named the surah by its opening words when he told Ubayy ibn Kaʿb that God commanded him to recite it; Ubayy asked whether he had been named and wept. It is commonly called “Lam yakun” in tafsir and hadith books and in Tunisian Qur’an schools.
rows.anchor: روى البخاري ومسلم عن أنس بن مالك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah has six reported titles: al-Qayyimah in many muṣḥafs and some tafsirs, al-Bayyinah in some muṣḥafs, Ahl al-Kitab in Ubayy’s muṣḥaf, al-Bariyyah, and al-Infikak, alongside Lam yakun.
rows.anchor: فهذه ستة أسماء

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya says the better-known position among most commentators is that the surah is Meccan; Ibn al-Zubayr and ʿAtaʾ ibn Yasar say it is Medinan.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية : الأشهر أنها مكية

rows.speaker: القرطبي
rows.claim: Al-Qurtubi reverses the attribution: most commentators and Ibn ʿAbbas call it Medinan, while Yahya ibn Salam says Meccan.
rows.anchor: وعكس القرطبي فنسب القول بأنها مدنية إلى الجمهور وابن عباس

rows.speaker: أبو حبة البدري
rows.claim: Abu Hubba al-Badri reports Gabriel saying that God commanded the Prophet to recite this surah to Ubayy, who was a Medinan; Ibn Kathir transmits it from Ahmad.
rows.anchor: بسنده إلى أبي حبة البدري

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn Ashur prefers a Medinan date because the surah repeatedly criticizes the People of the Book and because of Abu Hubba’s report; al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, and Jabir ibn Zayd also classify it as Medinan.
rows.anchor: وهو الأظهر لكثرة ما فيها من تخطئة أهل الكتاب ولحديث أبي حبة البدري

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAtiyya argues that the Prophet only engaged the People of the Book in disputation at Medina.
rows.anchor: ابن عطية : إن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم إنما دفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the revelation order it is 101st, after al-Talaq and before al-Hashr, placing its revelation around late year three or early year four before the Banu Nadir campaign.
rows.anchor: وقد عدت المائة وإحدى في ترتيب النزول نزلت بعد سورة الطلاق وقبل سورة الحشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most count eight verses in the surah, while the people of Basra count nine.
rows.anchor: وعدد آياتها ثمان عند الجمهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah rebukes polytheists and the People of the Book for rejecting the Quran and Messenger, exposes their inconsistency in rejecting the proof they awaited, refutes their claim that God mandated their existing religions, warns them of punishment, declares disbelievers the worst creation, and praises believers with eternal reward and divine pleasure.
rows.anchor: توبيخ المشركين وأهلل الكتاب على تكذيبهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It also praises the Quran for including what earlier revealed books contained and adding further merit.
rows.anchor: تنويه بالقرآن وفضله على غيره باشتماله على ما في الكتب الإلاهية

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Al-Fakhr quotes al-Wahidi calling the opening verse among the Quran’s most difficult in structure and interpretation, saying even leading scholars have floundered; al-Fakhr says he has not yet summarized the problem.
rows.anchor: ذكر الفخر عن الواحدي في ( التفسير البسيط ) له

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Al-Fakhr’s apparent reading is that disbelievers would leave disbelief when the proof, the Messenger, came, whereas verse 4 says the People of the Book only split after the proof arrived, apparently worsening their disbelief.
rows.anchor: تقتضي أنهم صاروا منفكين عن كفرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the surface, verse 1’s implied promise that the disbelievers leave unbelief at the Messenger’s coming contradicts verse 4’s statement that the People of the Book divided only after the proof came.
rows.anchor: حصل بين الآية الأولى والآية الثانية مناقضة في الظاهر

rows.speaker: الفخر
rows.claim: Al-Fakhr’s difficulty assumes “Messenger from God” apposes “the proof” and that the omitted complement of “cease” is disbelief; “until” would then imply they leave disbelief upon the Messenger’s arrival.
rows.anchor: لدلالة الكلام عليه لأنهم لما أجريت عليهم صلة الذين كفروا دل ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The standard connection treats the People of the Book’s division as their turning away from Islam, which increases their disbelief by multiplying misleading doubts despite a shared root of unbelief.
rows.anchor: فإن تفرقهم راجع إلى تفرقهم عن الإسلام وهو ازدياد في الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further problem is that history shows no disbelievers ever abandoned unbelief, while the subjunctive after “until” signals a future arrival even though the Messenger had come years before this revelation and they persisted in disbelief.
rows.anchor: أن المشاهدة دلت على أن الذين كفروا لم ينفكوا عن الكفر في زمن ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because the apparent wording and construction fail, the passage must be read nonliterally, either by shifting the sentence’s pragmatic meaning or by shifting a word to metaphor or metonymy.
rows.anchor: إما بصرف تركيب الخبر عن ظاهر الإخبار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Exegetes propose about fifteen solutions, which Ibn Ashur groups into five: read the whole sentence as rebuke and astonishment (al-Farraʾ, Naftawayh, al-Zamakhshari); interpret “cease” as leaving divine respite for punishment (Ibn ʿAtiyya); or supply different complements to “cease”—disbelief (ʿAbd al-Jabbar), agreement in disbelief (al-Fakhr, Abu Hayyan), testimony before the mission (Ibn Kaysan al-Asamm), or life itself (some linguists).
rows.anchor: تأويل الجملة بأسرها بأن يؤول الخبر إلى معنى التوبيخ والتعجيب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Two further approaches make “until” mean a conditional “even if,” or make the Messenger an angel bringing a heavenly book; the latter is Abu Muslim’s view as reported by al-Fakhr and implies mockery.
rows.anchor: بأنه رسول من الملائكة يتلو عليهم صحفا من عند الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Alusi records most proposed views and al-Qurtubi most of the remainder without attribution; the proposals overlap, so Ibn Ashur says their details can be mapped to his five categories.
rows.anchor: وقد تعددت أقوال المفسرين فبلغت بضعة عشر قولا ذكر الآلوسي أكثرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book” means those who disbelieved in Muhammad’s message, as in the verse about the hypocrites’ allies.
rows.anchor: أنهم كفروا برسالة محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم مثل ما في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim circulated among both groups before the Prophet came, so the future “until the proof comes” fits their former refrain: they would not leave their religion until a promised sign arrived; this prepares for the Messenger described next.
rows.anchor: أنهم كانوا يقولون ذلك قبل مجيء الرسول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here “proof” means the sign they claimed to await, a promised proof from their perspective, not a later event that caused them to abandon disbelief.
rows.anchor: أنكم كنتم تقولون لا نترك ما نحن عليه من الدين حتى تأتينا البينة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Infikak” means release or departure, from the transitive verb for separating; its omitted complement is disbelief, supplied by the description of the people as disbelievers.
rows.anchor: فالانفكاك : الإقلاع ، وهو مطاوع فكه إذا فصله وفرقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim came from Jews in Medina and nearby settlements, passed to Meccan polytheists who consulted them for a defense of rejecting Islam, and also included surrounding Arab tribes and individual Christians.
rows.anchor: فهذا القول صادر من اليهود الذين في المدينة والقرى التي حولها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran documents Jews’ claimed condition that they would believe only in a messenger whose sacrifice fire consumed, and their later rejection of a confirming book they already recognized.
rows.anchor: وقد حكى الله عن اليهود أنهم قالوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It records Jesus’ prophecy of Ahmad and the Christians’ rejection when he came with clear proofs, as well as the People of the Book’s jealous wish to return believers to disbelief.
rows.anchor: وحكى عن النصارى بقوله تعالى حكاية عن عيسى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The polytheists likewise rejected the Messenger by demanding signs like those given to earlier messengers or like Moses’ sign.
rows.anchor: وحكى عن المشركين بقوله : { فلما جاءهم الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The choice of “proof” may translate a phrase from the People of the Book’s scriptures, perhaps Matthew’s “testimony to all nations”; its repetition may reflect that specific resonance.
rows.anchor: لعل إيثار التعبير بها هنا لأنها أحسن ما تترجم به العبارة الواقعة في كتب أهل الكتاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite “the proof” may be a generic mental definite, functioning like an indefinite “a proof,” as in the expression “enter the market”; Zuhayr’s line similarly uses “war” generically.
rows.anchor: تعريف العهد الذهني ، وهو أن يراد معهود بنوعه لا بشخصه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it may refer to the proof familiar to them, their prophets’ promises, though their imagined versions differed; the Quran repeatedly uses this word for the anticipated, clear proof.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون التعريف لمعهود عند المخبر عنهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The partitive “min” in “among the People of the Book” explains which disbelievers are meant.
rows.anchor: و { من } في قوله : { من أهل الكتاب } بيانية بيان للذين كفروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The People of the Book precede the polytheists despite the latter’s graver disbelief because they had priority in circulating the anticipated-proof argument and gave a more learned denial of Muhammad’s prophethood; unlettered polytheists sought their counterarguments, especially after the Hijra.
rows.anchor: فلما صدمتهم الدعوة المحمدية فزعوا إلى اليهود ليتلقوا منهم ما يردون به تلك الدعوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earlier scriptures promised a messenger with a law and a book confirming previous revelation, evoking the Torah’s promise to put God’s words in his mouth, the Gospel’s promise to remind people of Jesus’ words, and the Quran’s statement of confirmation.
rows.anchor: وفي هذا تذكير بغلطهم فإن كتبهم ما وعدت إلا بمجيء رسول معه شريعة وكتاب مصدق لما بين يديه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ghazali says Muhammad’s combined virtues reached the level of a miracle and his many miracles were exceptionally manifest.
rows.anchor: قال حجة الإسلام في كتاب ( المنقذ من الضلال ) : ( إن مجموع الأخلاق الفاضلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “From God” modifies “messenger,” rather than forming a genitive construction, allowing “messenger” to take a tanwin that magnifies him.
rows.anchor: ولم يسلك طريق الإضافة ليتأتى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Reciting purified pages” is a second adjective or circumstantial clause and embeds praise of the Quran, since the promised messenger is not elsewhere described as reciting pages.
rows.anchor: صفة ثانية أو حال ، وهي إدماج بالثناء على القرآن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Reciting” means repeating words without addition or omission, whether read from writing or memory, indicating that the Prophet reads the unchanged revealed wording aloud.
rows.anchor: إعادة الكلام دون زيادة عليه ولا نقص منه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Pages” are writing sheets of parchment, leather, or cloth; calling the revelation pages is prospective metonymy because God commanded it to be written, like “I see myself pressing wine.”
rows.anchor: مجاز بعلاقة الأيلولة لأنه مأمور بكتابته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording implies that God commanded the Quran to be written on sheets and other materials such as shoulder blades, scraps, and stones; it is called a book because it is written and recited.
rows.anchor: أن الله أمر رسوله صلى الله عليه وسلم بكتابة القرآن في الصحف
